raw_response:
I'm 40 years old and I've been farming our land in Quzhou County since I finished middle school. My family has about 8 mu, which is more than some but we manage it ourselves with hired help at harvest time. I don't gamble with the cropping system — every year I plant winter wheat in October and then summer corn right after the wheat comes off in early June. That's what this land is good for, and the grain buyers always show up.

For wheat seed, I buy improved varieties from the supply shop in town. Last year I used a Shimai variety and it did fine, gave me about 1000 jin per mu. For corn, I always use hybrid seed — probably Nongda or Denghai, whatever the shop has at a decent price this year. My cousin planted a new hybrid last summer and got over 1200 jin per mu, so spending a bit more on hybrid corn seed is worth it.

Fertilizer is where I don't take risks. The extension fellow came through last spring telling everyone to cut nitrogen to 15 kg per mu, but I tried reducing two years ago and the wheat turned yellow at jointing stage. I lost sleep over it. Never again. I put down about 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu before wheat planting, and then topdress with urea in the spring when I see how the wheat looks. All together that's about 20 kg nitrogen, 8 kg phosphorus, and 3 kg potassium per mu for wheat. For corn I use less — around 18 kg nitrogen, 4 kg phosphorus, 3 kg potassium — because corn doesn't need as much fuss if the summer rains come on time.

Water costs keep going up. The electricity bill for pumping from our tube well gets higher every year, and the village committee is talking about raising the fee again. But wheat is picky — I'll irrigate four times: right after sowing to help it sprout, once before winter freeze-up so the seedlings don't dry out, once at jointing in March, and once more at grain filling if May is dry. For corn I rely more on the summer rains and irrigate twice, once when the seedlings are small and once at the big ear stage.

I plough the wheat field in October to break up the soil after the corn stubble. For corn there's no time — from wheat harvest to corn planting is maybe a week, sometimes less if it rains. Everyone uses no-tillage now, just plant right into the wheat stubble with the machine. 

For chemicals, I spray wheat three times — herbicide in early spring, then insecticide for aphids, and fungicide if I see rust spots. Corn gets two sprays, herbicide once and insecticide for corn borer once. I hate spending money on chemicals, but losing half a crop to bugs or weeds is much worse.

If the weather is normal I expect about 500 kg per mu for wheat and 550 kg per mu for corn. That's not the highest yield in the village but it's steady. My daughter is in high school in town and the fees aren't cheap, so I can't afford to gamble on new crops or cut my inputs too thin. Better to stick with what I know and lock in a decent harvest.
